solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Contentious posh girl gobbled pathetic Bale

parts.note: a deb (debutante) is an upper-class girl making her entrance into society

indicators.note: something pathetic is in a sorry, broken state, so these letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: to gobble is to eat greedily, so gobbled is ate
the footballer's name, taken as letters

explanation.surface: A snooty young woman wolfs down the sorry footballer Gareth Bale, which some might find a contentious menu.
explanation.walkthrough: DEB + ATE + ABLE gives DEBATEABLE, a less common spelling of debatable. Bale is a capital letter only for the surface's sake.
explanation.definitionFit: Something open to argument and dispute can be called contentious, and that is exactly what a debatable point is.

clue.text: All right, idiots turning up pissed?

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning upward means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: OK is the everyday short form of all right
a nit is British slang for a fool

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the fools staggering in are drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: OK and NITS together read upwards give STINKO. Pissed is British slang for drunk, not angry as in American usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Stinko is slang for heavily drunk, and in British English pissed means intoxicated rather than annoyed.

clue.text: Plant inside arsehole — and erection!

indicators.note: the letters sought sit within the run of words that follows, not as a whole word

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the next two

explanation.surface: A crude Private Eye gag about a plant lodged somewhere rude, with an exclamation of arousal.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the dash and read straight through: arseh-OLE AND ER-ection.
explanation.definitionFit: The oleander is a poisonous evergreen flowering shrub of the Mediterranean, a familiar garden plant.

clue.text: Old man's appearing in Hair — it's a sin!

indicators.note: to appear in something is to be found inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair
pa is a father, the old man, and the 's adds an S

explanation.surface: A disapproving father complains that the musical Hair is sinful.
explanation.walkthrough: Hair is the 1960s hippy musical famous for its nude scene, which makes the surface's moral outrage plausible; here it is just a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Trespass is an old word for wrongdoing, as in the Lord's Prayer's 'forgive us our trespasses', so it can mean a sin.

clue.text: see 8dn.
After recess, Tory right-wingers were at the helm (given a makeover)

indicators.note: this word sets the order of the parts, putting one directly behind another

parts.note: a recess is a break, a rest from work

indicators.note: the wing on the right of a word is its final letter, so only that end is kept

parts.note: the rightmost letter of the word
to be at the helm is to lead, so were at the helm is led

explanation.surface: Once Parliament's summer break is over, the Tory right is back in charge, freshly repackaged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory right-wingers' looks like a political faction, but it only asks for the right-hand letter of Tory. A recess is the parliamentary holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: To restyle something is to change its look or presentation, which is exactly what a makeover does.

clue.text: Balls-up by holy court, producing show

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top

parts.note: Ed Balls is a former Labour cabinet minister
pi is slang for pious
CT is the standard abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A church court makes a mess of things and ends up putting on a spectacle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls-up' reads as British slang for a mess; split it and Balls is Ed Balls, the Labour politician, written upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To depict is to portray or represent, which is one meaning of the verb to show.

clue.text: Terrible Thor rides! Prepare to back off!

indicators.note: the words must shed letters at their edges, leaving only a run from the middle

parts.note: drop the outer letters of the two words and read straight through

explanation.surface: The thunder god charges into battle, and everyone is warned to retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: tHOR RIDes: the answer straddles the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Horrid and terrible are both everyday adjectives for something very bad or unpleasant, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: (& 5dn./24ac.) Principals are going to be revolutionary? Expect sackings!

parts.note: school principals are head teachers
a modal verb marking the future, like are going to
to revolve, turning over and over

explanation.surface: If school leaders start a revolution, there will be dismissals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests politics, but here it just means turning round and round.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says people will be punished or dismissed, so it predicts sackings.

clue.text: Once more tossing away a good poll victory

indicators.note: throwing something out means a piece is removed from the word

parts.note: once more is a synonym of again
taken as written; this is what is thrown out

explanation.surface: A party wins a seat back after earlier losing it.
explanation.walkthrough: AGAIN loses its first A.
explanation.definitionFit: In election reporting, a seat captured from another party is called a gain, a welcome result for the winner.

clue.text: Almost achieve an erection during shock examination

indicators.note: something taking place during another is within it, so one piece sits inside

parts.note: to appal is to shock or horrify

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut

parts.note: to erect something is to raise it

explanation.surface: A man nearly gets aroused during an alarming medical inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erection' tempts you towards ER, but the phrase stands for a verb of lifting, cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: An appraisal is an assessment or evaluation of something, which is a kind of examination.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) Worry associated with covid-19 — another indication that you're on your way out?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a renewed surge of infections after the first one

definitions.text: another indication that you're on your way out
definitions.meaning: waving goodbye one more time as you leave

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes a wave literally as a hand signal of farewell; 'another' supplies the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Epidemiologists used the phrase for a fresh rise in cases, while a repeated hand gesture when leaving is literally another farewell gesture.

clue.text: TV series causes part-time politician to lose heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, so losing it means the central letters go

parts.note: casual work is part-time or irregular
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A television drama makes an MP who only works part-time feel discouraged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose heart' sounds like despair, but it means removing the middle two letters of the politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Casualty is a long-running BBC drama set in a hospital accident and emergency department.

clue.text: Crushed Trump's losing, um, tan — network brought in, which could go to his head?

definitions.text: which could go to his head

indicators.note: bringing something in puts it inside, so one piece goes within the other
something crushed is broken up and reshaped, so the letters are rearranged
to lose something is to be without it, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: the name with its possessive S, taken as letters
taken as written; these are removed
taken as written
a LAN is a local area network

explanation.surface: Mocking Trump's fake tan and suspiciously styled hair, the clue hints at something done to his scalp.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'um' is a real piece of fodder to remove, not a hesitation; what is left of the name joins the tan before shuffling, and the network goes in near the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A hair transplant moves follicles onto a balding scalp, so such a procedure is something that might end up on a man's head.

clue.text: Time to stick knackered Boris's establishment

indicators.note: sticking something into another places it inside
knackered is British slang for broken or worn out, so the letters are wrecked into a new order

parts.note: the name taken as letters
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: It is time to take down the worn-out establishment run by Boris Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: BORIS is shuffled to BISRO and T goes in the middle. Establishment looks political but is a business premises.
explanation.definitionFit: A bistro is a small, informal restaurant, and a restaurant or shop is often called an establishment.

clue.text: Be an MP and mean to stay put!

parts.note: an MP sits in Parliament, holding a seat
a mean person is tight with money

explanation.surface: A stingy member of Parliament intends to stay firmly in their seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like a verb meaning intend, but it is the adjective for stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit tight is an idiom for staying where you are and waiting without moving or acting.

clue.text: Administered doses before a port

indicators.note: this sets the order, putting one part in front of the next
administered means dealt out or handled, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Medicine is given out before a ship reaches harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Administered doses' reads naturally as medicine given, which hides the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Odessa is a major Black Sea seaport city in southern Ukraine.

clue.text: Being stressed out, crumbles?

indicators.note: out suggests things put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as letters

explanation.surface: Someone under too much pressure finally falls apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumbles' looks like a verb for collapsing; it is the plural of the pudding. Stressed simply written backwards is the same word, a famous coincidence.
explanation.definitionFit: A crumble is a baked fruit pudding topped with crumbly pastry, so crumbles are examples of puddings; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Lighter, just going round about

parts.note: just and fair both mean equitable

indicators.note: turning round makes something face the other way, so letters read backwards

parts.note: re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Someone describes a lighter that is simply being passed around.
explanation.walkthrough: Lighter is the comparative adjective, not a cigarette lighter.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair describes pale hair or skin, so fairer means paler in colour, which is lighter.

clue.text: Contribution to a column: "Evert played with support"

indicators.note: something played with is fiddled about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the tennis star's name taken as letters
a bra is a supporting undergarment

explanation.surface: A newspaper column item about the tennis champion Chris Evert playing in a sports bra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Column' looks journalistic but is the spinal column. Chris Evert is an American tennis great.
explanation.definitionFit: Each vertebra is one of the small bones that together make up the spine, so it is a part of the spinal column.

clue.text: Cry "LibDem's leader's gone down!"

indicators.note: something gone has been removed, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: to bellow is to cry out loudly

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the party name

explanation.surface: A shout goes up that the Liberal Democrat party leader has lost an election or fallen.
explanation.walkthrough: BELLOW loses one of its Ls. The Liberal Democrats are a UK political party.
explanation.definitionFit: Below and down are both adverbs meaning at or to a lower position, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Coy at first, the bloke's into S & M, causing rupture

indicators.note: going into something means being placed inside it

parts.note: the two letters, which go round the rest
his is the possessive belonging to a male person

indicators.note: at first points to the beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A shy man gets into sadomasochism, and it causes a split with his partner.
explanation.walkthrough: C and HIS sit between S and M, which here are just two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A schism is a split or division, especially within a church or group, which is a rupture between factions.

clue.text: Who had an eyeful of almost erect veteran?

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the final letter is cut

parts.note: hard can mean stiff and upright
a veteran is someone old and experienced

explanation.surface: A rude question about who got an eyeful of an aroused old soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: King Harold is traditionally said to have been killed at the Battle of Hastings in 1066 by an arrow in the eye, so he literally had an eyeful.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bayeux Tapestry tradition shows the English king struck in the eye by an arrow, making the cryptic phrase a punning description.

clue.text: Legal injunction, substantial, presented THUS?

parts.note: a writ is a written court order
substantial and large both mean big

explanation.surface: A big court order is served in shouting capitals.
explanation.walkthrough: THUS is printed in capitals, so it is literally shown in big letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Writ large means displayed in an exaggerated or very obvious way, and capital letters are one visible example.

clue.text: see 9ac.
see 8dn.
Maybe Panorama sets WHO off

parts.note: television sets are TVs

indicators.note: off suggests something gone wrong or out of place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the World Health Organization's initials, taken as letters

explanation.surface: A current affairs programme upsets the World Health Organization.
explanation.walkthrough: Panorama is the BBC's long-running investigative current affairs programme; 'Maybe' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Panorama is a television programme, so it is one example of a broadcast on the small screen.

clue.text: Speaking of Labour leader being into hunting out pests

indicators.note: being into something means being placed inside it

parts.note: ratting is hunting rats

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the party name

explanation.surface: A remark about the Labour leader being keen on pest control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being into' looks like enthusiasm but asks for one piece to go inside the other: L inside RATTING.
explanation.definitionFit: Rattling, as in rattling on, means talking quickly and at length, so it is a lively kind of chatter.
